summary: Defines an SMTP service extension that lets a client mark a message so it can be tracked later. This helps find the status of undelivered mail if no delivery or disposition notice arrives.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like putting a tracking sticker on a package at the post office so you can ask later where it is.

questions: how to track email through smtp
what is the mtrk smtp extension
how long do mail servers keep tracking data
subtitle: A way for a sender to tag an outgoing email so its fate can be looked up later if no delivery notice ever arrives.

tldr.problem: Sometimes a sender never gets a delivery or read notification for a message and has no way to learn where it went.
tldr.mechanism: The SMTP client adds an MTRK parameter to the MAIL command, carrying a hash of a secret random number, plus a globally unique ENVID. Servers keep the hash for a while so later tracking queries can be authenticated.
tldr.outcome: Message tracking is meant as a last resort when DSNs and MDNs do not answer the question. The RFC updates RFC 3461.

today: RFC 3885 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3461. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Role
sections.content:
RFC 3885 defines an SMTP service extension that lets a client mark a message for future tracking. The overall model is described in a companion document, and the query side is the Message Tracking Query Protocol (RFC 3887, model in RFC 3888).

The RFC calls a tracking query a last resort. Normally, Delivery Status Notifications (DSNs, RFC 3461) and Message Disposition Notifications (MDNs, RFC 3798) give the primary delivery status. Only if the message is not received, or neither mechanism answers, should a tracking query be issued.
sections.plainLanguage: Tracking is what you do when the usual 'it arrived' notes never show up. You only ask the post office after you have waited and heard nothing.

sections.title: The Extension at a Glance
sections.content:
The extension is named Message Tracking and is announced with the EHLO keyword MTRK. No parameters are allowed on that keyword, though future documents may add some. It follows the SMTP service extension mechanism of RFC 1869.

It adds one optional MTRK parameter to the MAIL command. The ENVID parameter of MAIL and the ORCPT parameter of RCPT from RFC 3461 MUST also be supported, with all their RFC 3461 meaning. No new SMTP verbs are defined.

The maximum length of a MAIL command line grows by 40 characters for the MTRK keyword and value. The 107 characters for ENVID and the 507 characters for ORCPT that RFC 3461 requires must be allowed too.
sections.plainLanguage: The mail servers say 'I know how to do tracking' with a special word. After that, the sender can add one extra label to the envelope.

sections.title: The MTRK Parameter
sections.content:
To make a message trackable, the sender creates two values: A, a large random number, and B, the SHA-1 hash of A. A MUST be at least 128 bits and MUST NOT be more than 1024 bits. The sender base64 encodes B and sends it as the mtrk-certifier.

mtrk-parameter  = "MTRK=" mtrk-certifier [ ":" mtrk-timeout ]
mtrk-certifier  = base64
mtrk-timeout    = 1*9DIGIT

A stays in the originator's tracking database and is used to validate future tracking requests. B is stored by compliant receiving MTAs and used to authenticate those requests.

The optional mtrk-timeout is the number of seconds the client asks servers to keep the tracking data, counted from the first receipt at each server. Servers MAY ignore it if it violates local policy, and MAY enforce an upper limit, which MUST be at least one day. Without a timeout, the local default SHOULD be 8-10 days and MUST be at least one day. The data MUST NOT expire while the message is still in that server's queue.

When relaying to another compliant server, the MTA SHOULD pass a timeout equal to the remaining life of the tracking information, reduced by the seconds the message sat at this MTA. If the result is zero or less, the whole MTRK parameter MUST NOT be passed on and the tracking path is considered lost.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender keeps a secret code and gives the post office only a scrambled version of it. Later, showing the real code proves you are the sender. The post office also only keeps its notes for a limited time.

sections.title: Unique Message Identifiers with ENVID
sections.content:
Tracking needs an identifier that no other message ever shares. So if MTRK is given, an ENVID parameter MUST be included, with the RFC 3461 syntax extended to unique-envid = local-envid "@" fqhn. The value MUST be chosen so that no other message from this or any other system ever uses it. Usually fqhn is the sender's fully qualified host name and local-envid is an identifier that host never reuses.

If local-envid, fqhn and the at sign together exceed the acceptable ENVID length of 100, the fqhn SHOULD be replaced by its SHA-1 encoded in base64. That is a 27 octet string, which leaves 72 octets for local-envid. The RFC warns that sequential integers are likely to collide with other hosts, while a SHA-1 of the time of day, the host's IP address and a random number is unlikely to.

Any resubmission of the message MUST get a new ENVID. This includes forwarding or resending from a user agent, but not MTA-level aliasing or forwarding where the message never leaves the transmission system.
sections.plainLanguage: Every parcel needs a number nobody else will ever use. If you ship it again, it gets a brand new number.

sections.title: Forwarding Tracking Certifiers
sections.content:
MTAs SHOULD pass unexpired certifiers along during normal hop-to-hop transfers. If the next MTA does not support MTRK, the MTRK= parameter MUST be deleted. If it supports DSNs, ENVID and ORCPT MUST NOT be deleted.

If aliasing or forwarding ends with exactly one recipient, the MTA SHOULD treat it as an ordinary hop and forward MTRK, ENVID and ORCPT unchanged, apart from decrementing the timeout.

If a redirection produces more than one recipient, the MTA MUST NOT copy the certifier. It MAY pick one recipient as the primary one to which tracking requests go, and the others MUST NOT receive certifiers. MTAs MUST NOT forward MTRK certifiers when doing mailing list expansion.
sections.plainLanguage: If a letter is simply passed on to one new address, the tracking sticker goes with it. If it gets copied to many people, only one copy may keep the sticker, and a mailing list gets none.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker could try to flood a server's database by submitting many small tracked messages. In that case a site may lower its maximum retention period retroactively.

The secret value A must be hard to predict and not reused, and the originating client must protect it. For example, if it is stored in a message store such as a Sent folder, the client must make sure attackers cannot reach it, particularly on a shared store.

Sites also balance hiding internal names and topology against providing useful tracking. Some may treat delivery to an alias such as postmaster or webmaster as final delivery to avoid exposing individuals; others want tracking through an alias. Implementors are encouraged to let administrators choose.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep your secret code safe, because anyone who finds it could ask about your mail. Post offices also need to be careful not to reveal who works behind a shared mailbox.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The only IANA action noted in the RFC is that IANA has registered the SMTP extension defined in section 3. That is the Message Tracking extension with the MTRK EHLO keyword.

The response format that goes with this extension, the message/tracking-status content type, is defined separately in RFC 3886.
sections.plainLanguage: The new feature was written in the official list of mail features so everyone uses the same name for it.

data.title: ABNF for the MTRK parameter
data.code:
mtrk-parameter  = "MTRK=" mtrk-certifier [ ":" mtrk-timeout ]
mtrk-certifier  = base64        ; authenticator
mtrk-timeout    = 1*9DIGIT      ; seconds until timeout
